The draft under the walnut tree

Thursday, 13 August, in Grandpa Gheorghe's village. A Madrid newspaper has asked Ecaterina for an 800-word opinion article: "Do handwritten letters still make sense?". She reads the draft under the walnut tree. Marta and doña Remedios, who has arrived from Seville, are listening.
I begin like this: "In my opinion, handwritten letters not only still make sense, but today they are more necessary than ever."
A good thesis. Clear from the first line. And what is your first argument?
That a letter can be kept. It must not be forgotten that a letter can wait forty years in a drawer. An email gets lost in a week.
That is undeniable. But someone will tell you that letters are slow and that nobody has time today.
For that I have the counterargument: "Although it is true that email is faster, speed is not always a virtue."
And are you going to talk about my grandfather?
Without names. Some people think opinion articles must be impersonal. I believe a real example convinces more than ten statistics.
I agree. But watch the length: eight hundred words are very few for forty years.
That is why the conclusion will be very short: "For all the reasons given, I believe we must keep writing letters. And, above all, sending them."
The last sentence is the headline. "The letters we don't send."

In the DELE B2, the writing task usually asks for 150–180 or 180–220 words. Respect the length: a text that is far too long loses points just like one that is too short.
2. Expressing opinion in the formal register
In my opinion, letters still make sense.
From my point of view, speed is not always a virtue.
I am convinced that a real example convinces more.
I don't think email can replace a letter.
Remember the rule from chapter 71: "creo que / considero que / estoy convencido de que" + indicative; "no creo que / no considero que" + subjunctive.
3. The counterargument and its rebuttal
Although it is true that email is faster, speed is not always a virtue.
Some people think writing by hand is a waste of time; however, it is precisely that time that gives a letter its value.
Letters may be slow. Nevertheless, what matters is not when they arrive, but that they arrive.
A well-refuted counterargument makes a text more convincing than three arguments with no objection at all. It shows you have thought about the other side too.
4. The conclusion and the title
In conclusion, a letter is not a message: it is an object that is kept.
In short, it is not about writing more, but about writing better.

The conclusion brings no new arguments: it restates the thesis in other words and leaves the reader with an idea to remember. A good title is short and provocative, often a sentence from the conclusion.

In my opinion, handwritten letters not only still make sense, but today they are more necessary than ever. I say this as a translator, but also as someone who took forty years to send one.

First of all, a letter can be kept. It is undeniable that an email gets lost in a folder within a few weeks, while a letter can wait for decades in a drawer or between the pages of a book, until someone finds it.

Although it is true that writing by hand is slow, slowness is not a flaw: it is precisely the time you devote to a letter that gives it value. Some people think nobody has that time any more; however, we all find it when we really want to say something.
For all the reasons given, I believe we must keep writing letters. And, above all, sending them. Because the letters we don't send are left waiting too, and sometimes they wait longer than we do.

At the beginning of August, Ecaterina received an email from a Madrid newspaper. It was signed by the head of the opinion section, a former colleague of Begoña's. They were asking her for an eight-hundred-word article for the Sunday supplement of 30 August, on a topic that, in their view, only she could handle: "Do handwritten letters still make sense?". Ecaterina read the email three times. She had written a whole book, but never an opinion article. She told Ana that a book lets you tell a story; an article forces you to convince.

She accepted, of course. But in the first few days she wrote nothing. She started four drafts and threw them all away. In the first she told too much of the story and did not give her opinion at all. In the second she gave her opinion so much that it sounded like a sermon. In the third there were so many connectors that Mr Dan, who read it over her shoulder, said it looked like one of his tables. She began the fourth with "Dear reader" and threw it away before finishing the first line, because she felt she was writing a letter instead of an article about letters.

Marta, from Madrid, gave her another piece of advice on the phone. She told her that an opinion article is not a short book, but a conversation with someone who disagrees with you. That she had to imagine a specific reader, sceptical, a bit unfriendly, and write to convince him. Ecaterina asked her whom she imagined when she wrote. Marta answered that when she wrote novels she imagined her grandfather; but when she wrote articles she imagined Begoña, because if she managed to convince Begoña, she could convince anyone.

Costel, who had prepared for the C1 by writing one argumentative essay a week, offered to explain the structure to her. He did it in the truck cab, one Thursday afternoon, with a sheet of paper on the steering wheel. He drew her five boxes: introduction with thesis, first argument, second argument, counterargument with reply, and conclusion. Under each box he wrote the formulas Ana had taught him. Ecaterina looked at him smiling. She told him she had been translating essays for forty years and nobody had ever explained them to her so clearly. Costel turned as red as a lobster.

Mr Dan, not to be outdone, made a table. He titled it "Letters versus emails: advantages and disadvantages" and divided it into four columns: speed, cost, durability and emotion. Email won in the first three. In the fourth, the letter won ten to nil. He sent it to Ecaterina with a note: "From a technical point of view, email is superior. From my point of view, the letter. I leave the conclusion to you." Ecaterina replied that it was the most honest table she had ever seen in her life.

Meanwhile, in the village, Grandpa Gheorghe was preparing his birthday as if it were a wedding. He was turning ninety-seven on 15 August, the feast of the Assumption, and had decided that this year he wanted everyone under the walnut tree: those from Bucharest, those from Madrid, those from Seville. He had explicitly asked for Faustino and doña Remedios to come, because he wanted to meet a man who was getting married at eighty-seven. Elena had told him it was impossible, that some old people from Seville would not cross Europe for a birthday. Grandpa answered that she would see.

They came. Doña Remedios had never been on a plane, and Faustino only once, in 1970, to go to the Canary Islands. They flew from Seville to Madrid and from Madrid to Bucharest on 12 August, accompanied by Curro, who had instructions from his mother even more precise than the ones in May. Doña Remedios spent the take-off clinging to Faustino's hand. Faustino spent the take-off pretending he was not afraid. On landing at Otopeni, doña Remedios said that although it was true that flying was fast, there was nothing in the sky worth looking at. Faustino told her that he had only looked at her.

At the airport Ecaterina, Ana and Rosa Elena were waiting for them, with the same colourful sign from May, to which the girl had added a few words: "Bun venit, doña Remedios, the one with the lamp. Welcome, señor Faustino, the one with the beret." Faustino was indeed wearing the red beret, despite the thirty-five degrees in Bucharest. Doña Remedios stood looking at the sign for a long time and said nobody had ever waited for her at an airport, because she had never been in one. Then she hugged Rosa Elena and gave her a little fan, made to her size.

Marta and Andrei arrived the same day, on another flight. Pilar and Manuel on the 13th, from Seville. Carmen and Juan had been in Bucharest since the beginning of the month, spending the summer with Ana and Mihai. On the morning of the 13th they all set off for the village in three cars and Costel's truck, which carried the chairs, the tables, two huge watermelons and an amount of food that, according to Juan, would have fed a regiment. Doña Remedios sat in the truck cab next to Costel, because she had said she wanted to see Romania from above. Faustino was in the back of Mihai's car, carsick.

Grandpa Gheorghe was waiting for them at the gate, with his Sunday cap and his walking stick, freshly shaved, with no trace of the July pneumonia. When Faustino got out of the car, still pale, the two old men stood looking at each other for a moment without saying anything, because they had not a single word in common. Then Grandpa held out his hand and said, in the Spanish he had learned the summer before: "Por fin." Faustino shook his hand and answered, very seriously: "Salud." And from that moment they understood each other perfectly for four days, without anyone quite knowing how.

Andrei spent the afternoon photographing the two old men. Grandpa Gheorghe teaching Faustino to draw water from the well with the bucket. Faustino teaching Grandpa to wear the beret tilted, like the Madrileños of the old days. Both of them sitting on the porch, in silence, looking at the road. Begoña had once told him that the best photos were of people who did not know they were being photographed. Andrei sent Begoña one of those photos that evening. Begoña answered with a single word, the rarest in her vocabulary: "Lovely."

On the first evening, under the walnut tree, Ecaterina took out the fifth draft of the article. She had written it on the flight back from Madrid in May, in a notebook, and had kept correcting it over the summer without showing it to anyone. She read it aloud to Marta and doña Remedios after dinner, by the light of the bulbs Mihai had hung from the branches again. It began with a clear thesis: "In my opinion, handwritten letters not only still make sense, but today they are more necessary than ever." Marta said it was a good thesis. Doña Remedios said it was a brave thesis.

The first argument was that a letter can be kept. Ecaterina had not wanted to give names, but anyone who knew the story would have understood which letters she meant: one that had waited almost forty years in a drawer in Bucharest and another that had waited forty in a drawer in Madrid. Doña Remedios interrupted her to say that someone would tell her letters are slow and that nobody has time to write them today. Ecaterina smiled, because she had foreseen the objection. She read the counterargument she had written right after: "Although it is true that email is faster, speed is not always a virtue."

Marta asked her whether she would talk about her grandfather. Ecaterina answered: without names. She explained that some people think opinion articles must be impersonal, with data and statistics, but that she was convinced a single real example convinces more than ten statistics. Doña Remedios agreed, but warned her to watch the length: eight hundred words are very few for forty years. Ecaterina told her that was why the conclusion would be very short. And she read it: "For all the reasons given, I believe we must keep writing letters. And, above all, sending them."

Silence fell under the walnut tree. You could hear the crickets and, in the distance, a dog barking at another house in the village. Marta was the first to speak. She said the last sentence was the headline, that there was no need to look for another: "The letters we don't send." Ecaterina wrote it in the margin of the notebook. Faustino, who had listened to everything from the other end of the table without understanding almost anything, because he was teaching Grandpa Gheorghe to play mus, raised his head and asked whether the article was about Machado. They told him it wasn't. He said that, then, something was missing.

Later, much later, after the others had gone to bed, Ecaterina stayed alone on the porch with the notebook. She thought about what Faustino had said. She thought he was right, that the article was missing something, even if it wasn't Machado. It was missing why she had not sent her letter in 1987. She wrote it in a single sentence, in the margin: "Because I was afraid the answer would be worse than the silence." She read it several times. Then she decided she would not put it in the article. It was true, but it was hers. There are sentences that are not meant to convince anyone.

On 14 August, Ecaterina spent the whole morning under the walnut tree, correcting. She counted the words with her finger, as Costel did in exams. She had a hundred and twelve too many. She had to cut, as in January, and cutting hurt just as much as it had then. She took out a paragraph about stamps, another about her mother and a very beautiful sentence about the smell of paper that she liked a lot. Rosa Elena, sitting beside her with her drawing book, asked her why she was cutting so much. Ecaterina explained that an article is like a suitcase for a short trip: you must take only the bare essentials, even if the rest is beautiful too.

Meanwhile, Faustino and Grandpa Gheorghe had become inseparable. They walked together through the village, slowly, each with his stick, saying nothing to each other or saying things the other did not understand and nodding anyway. Grandpa showed him the well, the hens, the cemetery where his wife was buried and the school where he had learned to read as an adult. Faustino taught him to play mus with a pack of Spanish cards he had brought in his suitcase, just in case. Grandpa lost every game, but said it was the best game he had ever learned, because you don't have to talk to cheat.

Carmen and Mrs Florica, for their part, had turned Grandpa's kitchen into a peaceful battlefield. Carmen was teaching the village women to make tortilla, and they watched her with suspicion, because they did not understand how you could cook something with so few ingredients. Mrs Florica was teaching Carmen to make sarmale, and Carmen said it was like making a hundred little tortillas wrapped in leaves. Juan, sitting on a stool at the kitchen door, tasted everything that came out and always said the same thing, in his ten-word Romanian: "Bun. Foarte bun."

One afternoon, Grandpa asked Ecaterina to be his interpreter. He wanted to tell Faustino something important and could not say it with gestures. The three of them sat on the porch. Grandpa told Faustino, sentence by sentence, that he had married in 1955, that he had been married for forty-eight years and that his wife had died twenty years ago. He told him that in all that time he had regretted only one thing: all the times he had waited until the next day to tell her something nice. "Don't wait," he told him. "At our age, tomorrow is a luxury." Ecaterina translated the sentence and had to stop for a moment before finishing it.

Faustino was silent for a long time. Then he got up, slowly crossed the yard to where doña Remedios was sitting with Rosa Elena, teaching her to make a paper fan, and whispered something in her ear. Nobody ever found out what. Doña Remedios laughed with her head thrown back, like in the 1985 photo Faustino had taken of another woman forty years earlier, and tapped him lightly on the arm with the fan. Faustino came back to the porch and sat down next to Grandpa. Grandpa asked him with a gesture whether he had told her. Faustino nodded. Grandpa said: "Por fin."

On 15 August, the feast of the Assumption, Grandpa turned ninety-seven. In the morning they all went to the village church, like the year before. Doña Remedios, who was very devout, followed the service in Romanian without understanding anything, but crossed herself at exactly the right moments, copying Mrs Florica, who had come with her husband in Mr Dan's car. Then they ate under the walnut tree: sarmale, tortilla, fried fish that Manuel had cooked in a huge pan, zacuscă, jamón, cozonac and Mrs Florica's three-tier cake, which this time had two candles: a nine and a seven.

Like the year before, Grandpa asked Rosa Elena to blow out the candles and make the wish in his place. This time the girl did not say it aloud. She closed her eyes, blew and stayed silent for a moment. Everyone was waiting for her to say it, because Rosa Elena always said her wishes aloud. But she didn't. When Mihai asked her why, the girl explained, very seriously, that she had learned that wishes come true better if you don't tell them, just as letters arrive better if you send them. Ecaterina, hearing her, took the notebook out of her bag and wrote the sentence on the last page.

Pilar, who had been very quiet all those days, asked to speak during the meal. She thanked Grandpa for welcoming them into his home, in a Spanish that Ecaterina translated sentence by sentence. She told him her father had been a man who waited, and that seeing him, she understood that in that house, too, people knew how to wait. Grandpa answered no, that in his house nobody waited: you light a lamp and go on living, which is different. Pilar thought about that difference for the rest of the afternoon. Later she told Ecaterina it was the wisest thing she had heard in years.

The presents were simple. Faustino gave Grandpa a book of Machado's poems in Spanish, with a dedication that doña Remedios had corrected for him: "For Gheorghe, who taught me that tomorrow is a luxury." Grandpa could not read it, but he put it in the window, next to the oil lamp. Doña Remedios gave him a fan from Triana, which Grandpa used all afternoon with great dignity. And Costel gave him a very flat cardboard box. Inside was an empty frame. He explained it was for the C1 diploma, which had not arrived yet. Grandpa hung it on the wall that very day, empty.

That evening, at seven, Grandpa lit the oil lamp in the window, as he had done every evening since July. Ecaterina, on the porch, lit a candle beside it. Marta switched on her phone's torch. One by one, everyone under the walnut tree lit something: Costel, the light in the truck cab, parked on the road; Andrei, his camera's flash; Rosa Elena, a toy lamp her grandmother Carmen had given her. For a minute, Grandpa's yard filled with little lights. Then someone put on music, and Grandpa asked doña Remedios to dance. Faustino, for the first time in his life, was not jealous.

Curro, doña Remedios's grandson, also had his moment. That evening he took out his guitar and played under the walnut tree. First he played something flamenco, which made Mrs Florica start clapping without quite knowing when. Then he asked Grandpa to sing him a song from the village, and Grandpa sang, with his ninety-seven-year-old voice, a very old doina. Curro listened with his eyes closed, and on the second verse began to accompany it on the guitar, finding the chords by ear. Nobody spoke. Doña Remedios said later it had been like hearing two countries shake hands.

On 16 August, before everyone left, Ecaterina sent the article to the newspaper from the porch, using Andrei's phone, because in the village there was signal only in one particular corner of the yard, next to the well. It had exactly eight hundred words. In the email subject she wrote only the title: "Las cartas que no mandamos". The head of the opinion section replied an hour later with a two-line message: she wrote that she would not change a single comma and that, if she ever wanted to write another, the paper would be delighted to publish it.

Before going back to Seville, doña Remedios asked to spend an afternoon in Bucharest, at Ecaterina's home. She wanted to see the drawer. Ecaterina showed it to her: the third drawer of the desk, the bottom one, empty, with the rectangular mark of the envelope in the wood. Doña Remedios looked at it in silence, as she had looked at the green sign in Madrid. Then she opened her bag, took out the framed copy of the 1958 bookmark that Andrei had made for her and put it in the drawer. She told Ecaterina that a drawer that had kept a letter for so long should not stay empty. Ecaterina did not know what to say. She closed the drawer slowly.

The article appeared on Sunday, 30 August, on page two of the supplement, with a small photo by Andrei: the empty drawer from the book's cover. That Sunday, the paper received over four hundred letters from readers. Real letters, handwritten, which arrived for weeks in the newsroom's letterbox. The head of the opinion section kept forwarding them to El Mostrador in cardboard boxes, because she did not know what to do with them. Lola arranged them on the back shelf, under the lamp, next to the first copy of the book. She said they were letters that someone had finally sent.

One of those letters reached Bucharest, addressed to Ecaterina, forwarded by the paper. It had been written by a seventy-eight-year-old man from Zaragoza. He told her that after reading the article he had opened a drawer he had not opened for thirty years, taken out a letter he had written to his brother after a quarrel and never sent, and that very Monday he had gone to the post office to send it. His brother had phoned him on Thursday, crying. Ecaterina read the letter twice. Then she put it in "Rayuela", between the other two.

Dear Mrs Ionescu, I am not in the habit of writing to newspapers. In my opinion, people who write to newspapers have too much free time. However, your article has forced me to change my mind.

Write an opinion article (at least 280 words) on one of these topics: "Do young people still read?", "Is working from home a good thing?", "Should cars be banned from city centres?". Follow the structure: thesis, two arguments, refuted counterargument, conclusion, and give it a title.
I stated the thesis clearly in the first paragraph (a mi juicio, desde mi punto de vista, considero que).
I ordered the arguments (en primer lugar, además, asimismo) and supported them with examples.
I introduced a counterargument (si bien es cierto que…, hay quien piensa que…) and refuted it (sin embargo, no obstante).
I concluded with "por todo lo expuesto" or "en definitiva", without new arguments.
I used the indicative after "creo que" and the subjunctive after "no creo que" correctly, and gave the text a short title.
Do young people still read? In my opinion, young people read more than ever, even if not always what we expect.
Although it is true that they spend hours in front of their phones, it must not be forgotten that a large part of that time is spent reading.
